representations.text:
Your March 30–April 12 records stayed close to your 28-day baseline, without a sustained shift. Sleep averaged 471 versus 470 minutes, starting around 22:49 with a consistent 07:00 wake time. Weekend sleep averaged 468 versus 472 minutes on weekdays—a small reversal of baseline, based on four weekend nights.

Steps stayed near 8,000/day (8,008 versus 8,039). Active time increased modestly from 55.2 to 57.8 minutes, still starting at 21:00; intensity is unknown. Low movement remained similar (452 versus 450 minutes), in roughly 44–47-minute daytime blocks separated by five-minute gaps.

Resting heart rate remained within 55–57 bpm, averaging 55.9 versus 56.2. RMSSD averaged 40 ms in both periods, with a narrower current range (28–52 versus 26–54); weekday fluctuations remained larger than weekend fluctuations. Activity showed little relationship to the following night's sleep, and heart rate and RMSSD were only weakly related. All days and nights had valid records.

Your sleep changed sharply late in this window. The first eight wake dates had 474–485 minutes of sleep, slightly above your 28-day average of 471. On April 7–12, sleep fell to 385–392 minutes for six consecutive nights, across weekdays and the weekend, with no return observed. Starts shifted from around 22:49 at baseline to 00:08–00:15, while waking stayed at 07:00. The overall average of 441 minutes (30 fewer) understates this late change.

Active time became variable: six 90-minute sessions at 20:30–22:00 and eight 45-minute sessions at 17:30–18:15, versus 50–60 minutes starting at 21:00 previously. Its average rose from 55.6 to 64.3 minutes; intensity is unknown. Correctly aligned with the following night's sleep, the relationship was weak (r=-0.07); short sleep followed both schedules.

Steps rose slightly (8,088 versus 7,947/day), while low movement stayed near 449 minutes. Resting heart rate (56.4 versus 55.9 bpm) and RMSSD (45.7 versus 45.0 ms) remained close to baseline despite the sleep change. Records were complete.

Your sleep became repeatedly shorter, with returns between short nights. Six wake dates across both weeks, including weekends, recorded 385–392 minutes versus your 28-day average of 471. Each followed a 90-minute activity interval at 20:30–22:00. All seven observed nights following 45-minute intervals at 17:30–18:15 recorded 474–485 minutes. Sleep starts alternated between 00:08–00:15 and 22:35–22:46; waking stayed at 07:00. This recurring pattern explains the 441-minute average, 30 minutes below baseline, better than a steady decline.

Across 13 correctly aligned pairs, activity duration and following-night sleep were strongly inversely related (r=-1.00 rounded), unlike baseline. Timing and duration changed together, so these observations cannot separate their relationships or establish causation; intensity is unknown.

Active time averaged 64.3 versus 55.6 minutes, previously starting at 21:00. Steps rose slightly (8,088 versus 7,947/day), while low movement remained near 449 minutes. Resting heart rate (56.4 versus 55.9 bpm) and RMSSD (45.7 versus 45.0 ms) stayed close to baseline. Records were complete; tracking whether this repeated timing pattern continues could be useful.

Your steps increased substantially and stayed elevated throughout March 30–April 12: 7,927/day versus your 28-day baseline of 2,818, an increase of 5,109 (+181%). Every current day exceeded the baseline maximum of 3,023. Weekday steps eased within the window, but remained elevated; weekends averaged 8,126 versus 7,847 on weekdays, whereas baseline showed virtually no weekday/weekend difference.

This step increase did not coincide with more recorded active time: it averaged 55.3 versus 56.2 minutes, still starting at 21:00. Weekend active time fell to 52.5 from 57.3 minutes despite higher steps. Intensity is unknown. Low movement decreased slightly (447 versus 451 minutes), with daytime blocks still separated by five-minute gaps.

Sleep stayed close to baseline (469 versus 471 minutes), with a small downward trend, starts around 22:51 and unchanged 07:00 waking. Resting heart rate averaged 55.9 versus 56.2 bpm, and RMSSD stayed near 45 ms. Current steps and active time were weakly related; activity had little relationship to following-night sleep, and heart rate and RMSSD showed no correlation. All records were valid and complete.
